content: Herpes simplex labialis (HSL), commonly referred to as cold sores, is a widespread condition caused by the herpes simplex virus. It manifests as painful vesicular eruptions on the lips, which eventually form crusts. These lesions can lead to cosmetic concerns and significant psychosocial distress. There is currently no cure for HSL, and it tends to recur periodically. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions aimed at preventing HSL in individuals of all ages. The review included 32 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 2,640 immunocompetent participants and assessed 19 different treatments. The quality of evidence ranged from low to moderate for most outcomes, with some outcomes having very low-quality evidence. Oral Antiviral Agents: Short-term use (≤1 month) of oral aciclovir showed inconsistent results in preventing recurrent HSL. Two RCTs provided low-quality evidence that aciclovir 400 mg taken twice daily reduced recurrence (risk ratio [RR] 0.26, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.13 to 0.51; n = 177). However, one RCT using aciclovir 800 mg twice daily and two RCTs using 200 mg five times daily found no significant preventive effects (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.87; n = 237; moderate-quality evidence and RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.07; n = 66; low-quality evidence, respectively). Short-term use of valaciclovir and famciclovir also showed uncertain effects in reducing HSL recurrence. For valaciclovir, one RCT provided moderate-quality evidence (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.28; n = 125). Long-term use (>1 month) of oral antiviral agents demonstrated a reduction in HSL recurrence. One RCT provided low-quality evidence that long-term aciclovir reduced both clinical recurrences (1.80 vs. 0.85 episodes per participant over 4 months, P = 0.009) and virological recurrences (1.40 vs. 0.40 episodes per participant over 4 months, P = 0.003). Another RCT found that long-term valaciclovir reduced the incidence of HSL (0.09 fewer episodes per participant per month; n = 95). Additionally, a suppressive regimen of valaciclovir was more effective than an episodic regimen (mean difference [MD] -0.10 episodes per participant per month, 95% CI -0.16 to -0.05; n = 120). No increase in adverse events was observed with oral antiviral agents (moderate-quality evidence). Topical Antiviral Agents: Short-term use of topical antiviral agents did not prevent recurrent HSL. Two RCTs provided moderate-quality evidence that topical aciclovir 5% cream likely had little effect on preventing recurrence (pooled RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.72; n = 271). Similarly, one RCT found that topical foscarnet 3% cream had little effect (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.40; n = 295). The efficacy of long-term use of topical aciclovir cream was uncertain. One RCT reported fewer research-diagnosed recurrences with aciclovir cream compared to placebo (P < 0.05), but no significant differences in participant-reported recurrences (P ≥ 0.05). Another RCT found no preventive effect of 1,5-pentanediol gel over 26 weeks (P > 0.05). A third RCT reported that 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin 20% gel led to significantly more recurrences than placebo (P = 0.003). No increase in adverse events was associated with topical antiviral agents. Other Interventions: Sunscreen application significantly prevented HSL triggered by experimental ultraviolet (UV) light in two RCTs (pooled RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.33; n = 111). However, another RCT found that sunscreen did not prevent HSL induced by natural sunlight (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.25 to 5.06; n = 51). No adverse events were reported in these studies. Limited data suggested potential efficacy for thymopentin, low-level laser therapy, and hypnotherapy in preventing recurrent HSL, with only one or two RCTs available for each intervention. There was no evidence supporting the efficacy of lysine, LongoVital® supplementation, gamma globulin, herpes simplex virus (HSV) type I subunit vaccine, or yellow fever vaccine in preventing HSL. Levamisole and interferon showed no consistent efficacy and were associated with an increased risk of adverse effects, such as fever. Conclusions: The evidence suggests that long-term use of oral antiviral agents can reduce the recurrence of HSL, although the clinical benefit is modest. Importantly, no increased risk of adverse events was observed with these agents. In contrast, the evidence for topical antiviral agents and other interventions either showed no efficacy or was inconclusive in preventing HSL.
